solution_full: Let $n=13$. Use $r\binom{n}{r}=n\binom{n-1}{r-1}$ (the result behind the differentiation technique $\dfrac{d}{dx}(1+x)^{n}=n(1+x)^{n-1}$) and the symmetry $\binom{n}{r}=\binom{n}{n-r}$.

$\sum_{r}r\binom{n}{r}^{2}=\sum_{r}n\binom{n-1}{r-1}\binom{n}{n-r}=n\binom{2n-1}{n-1}$ by Vandermonde (lower indices add to $n-1$; equivalently the coefficient of $x^{n-1}$ in $(1+x)^{n-1}(1+x)^{n}$).

The condition is $n^{2}\binom{2n-2}{n-1}+\lambda\,n\binom{2n-1}{n-1}=0$. Since $\binom{2n-1}{n-1}=\dfrac{2n-1}{n}\binom{2n-2}{n-1}$, this gives $n^{2}+\lambda(2n-1)=0$, i.e. $\lambda=-\dfrac{n^{2}}{2n-1}$.
originality_note: New: a linear condition on the weighted sums of squares of binomial coefficients, solved by turning r C(n,r) into n C(n-1,r-1) inside a square and inside a product, then applying Vandermonde twice; n = 13 makes 2n - 1 = 25 so the answer terminates (way 5). Closest known: sum of r C(n,r)^2 = n C(2n-1,n-1) as a standalone result. Different because: both the first and second moment of C(n,r)^2 are needed and must be compared through the ratio of central coefficients.
blueprint_concepts: Binomial sums by the differentiation technique (sum of r.C_r, r^2.C_r)

concept_use.Properties of binomial Coefficients: Symmetry C(n,r) = C(n,n-r) and Vandermonde turn the sums into C(2n-1,n-1) and C(2n-2,n-1), and their ratio (2n-1)/n is a property of binomial coefficients.
concept_use.Binomial sums by the differentiation tec: r C(n,r) = n C(n-1,r-1) (the differentiation technique) gives sum r C(n,r)^2 and sum r^2 C(n,r)^2.
